To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IL-6 and IL-8, and to a lesser extent IL-10 and TNFa, are useful markers for neonatal septicaemic disease, that the cytokines can be used to predict the severity of the disease, that the IL-6 level at the time of diagnosis can be used to estimate the risk of mortality, and that the IL-10 level at the time when the diagnosis is made can be used to assess the risk of long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

in neonatal septicaemias the IL-6 levels are higher in cases of early onset than in late onset septicaemias and in cases of early and late onset septicaemia the IL-6 level is higher than the TNFa level.
the cytokine levels of IL-6, IL-8, TNF-a and IFNg in cord blood of neonates with early-onset septicaemia were significantly higher than in healthy newborns.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cytokine determin-ations in neonatal septicaemias are not ready for routine clinical use yet.
the cytokine IL-6 and the chemokines IL-8 and MCP-1 are good candidates as markers of neonatal sepsis.

cytokine determination in neonates with suspected sepsisa is a useful tool to help clinicians in their decision-making process, but the results should be interpreted with caution, and the clinical picture of the infant should always be taken into account.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the host cytokine response to neonatal septicaemias is a dynamic process.
cytokine levels are elevated in the early hours of neonatal sepsis and that they are higher in the more severe cases.
